speaker: Derek Lowe
title: Derek Lowe, PhD: A Medicinal Chemist’s Thoughts on Drug Discovery and the Future of Pharma
question: In drug discovery, why do machine learning and computational methods still struggle to dramatically reduce clinical trial failure rates?
guest: Right now, I am not confident at all, truly not. But that said, I see no reason why these technologies can't work. I don't see any mathematical, physics, or biology reason why you can't compute your way through some of these questions. It's just a very hard problem, and we don't really know how to do it yet. There's a huge amount of work going into this because of that 85% failure rate—if you could move to just failing three out of four times, that would be a huge improvement. Anything that helps predict success would be overwhelmingly useful, but it is extremely hard. In many cases, we don't even know what we would be turning those computational tools loose on. Like toxicity, for example: most of the toxicity problems that kill drugs are unexpected target effects that come out of the clear blue sky because we didn't realize the target did that thing. How are you going to compute this? Machine learning will only rearrange the knowledge you already have and find trends and patterns in it. What if it's knowledge that no one has yet?

points.core: Machine learning only extracts patterns from existing biological knowledge already in datasets.
points.note: Accept: ML interpolates over known training data, cannot predict unmapped mechanisms, or hits an epistemic data ceiling. Do not credit: generic claims that AI simply needs more compute or better algorithms.

points.core: Drug-killing clinical toxicities frequently arise from previously unknown biological target effects.
points.note: Accept: unanticipated in-vivo toxicities, surprise off-target interactions, or unrecognized on-target physiological roles killing candidates. Do not credit: vague mentions of side effects without noting they were unknown beforehand.

points.core: Researchers often do not even know which biological variables to model computationally.
points.note: Accept: inability to specify the right biological inputs, endpoints, or pathways to feed models. Do not credit: generic complaints about messy data formatting or small sample sizes alone.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core problem is that most clinical failures stem from things current models predict poorly: whether modulating a target actually changes human disease, and whether a compound is safe in a whole organism. Roughly 90% of drugs entering trials fail, mostly for lack of efficacy in Phase II/III or unexpected toxicity, not because the molecule binds poorly. ML excels at the upstream, data-rich tasks such as structure prediction, binding affinity, and molecule generation, but those were never the main bottleneck.

Several factors limit progress downstream. Human biology is poorly understood and causal target validation is hard; models trained on cell lines and animal data inherit those systems' weak translation to patients. High-quality human outcome data are scarce, noisy, biased toward published positives, and labelled slowly, since each clinical "data point" takes years and millions of dollars. Models also generalise badly to novel chemistry and biology, exactly where new drugs lie. Finally, trials fail for non-molecular reasons too: patient heterogeneity, poor endpoints, dosing, and commercial decisions.

So far, AI-discovered drugs show improved Phase I success, but no clear evidence yet of better Phase II efficacy rates.

points.why: The response ties poor clinical prediction to the limits of the biology represented in training data.

Models also generalise badly to novel chemistry and biology, exactly where new drugs lie.

points.why: The response identifies unexpected toxicity in living subjects as a major cause of clinical failure.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Machine learning and computational methods excel primarily at early-stage molecular optimization—predicting protein structures, screening chemical libraries, and refining binding affinity—rather than solving the core drivers of clinical attrition: lack of human efficacy and unexpected toxicity. Most Phase II and III trials fail not because a drug poorly engages its intended target, but because modulating that target fails to alter complex human disease or triggers systemic adverse effects.

Computational models remain bottlenecked by an incomplete understanding of multiscale human physiology and a severe translational data gap. Their training sets rely heavily on simplified *in vitro* assays and animal models, which frequently fail to capture the dynamic biological networks of genetically and environmentally diverse patients. Meanwhile, informative human clinical datasets—especially standardized negative results from failed trials—are small, noisy, and siloed behind proprietary barriers, limiting a model's ability to generalize to novel, first-in-class mechanisms. Consequently, computational tools bring better-engineered molecules to the clinic faster without de-risking the underlying target biology, complex pharmacokinetics, and patient heterogeneity that ultimately govern trial outcomes.

points.why: The response ties limited prediction of novel mechanisms to what the training data capture.
quotes: Their training sets rely heavily on simplified *in vitro* assays and animal models, which frequently fail to capture the dynamic biological networks of genetically and environmentally diverse patients.
limiting a model's ability to generalize to novel, first-in-class mechanisms

points.why: The response identifies unexpected clinical toxicity as a major cause of failure and links systemic adverse effects to target modulation.
quotes: core drivers of clinical attrition: lack of human efficacy and unexpected toxicity
modulating that target fails to alter complex human disease or triggers systemic adverse effects

points.why: The response describes incomplete physiological knowledge and gaps in training data without saying researchers often cannot identify which biological variables to model.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Most clinical trials fail because the drug doesn't work well enough in patients or turns out to be unsafe. Roughly 90% of candidates that enter trials fail, and about half of those failures come from lack of efficacy. Computational methods are mainly good at the early chemistry: finding molecules that bind a target, predicting properties, and shortening the time to a candidate. They are much weaker at the question trials actually answer, which is whether hitting that target changes the disease in people.

Several problems get in the way. Our understanding of disease biology is incomplete, so a drug can be "optimized" against the wrong target. The training data come mostly from cell assays and animal models that predict human outcomes poorly. Human outcome data are scarce, noisy and skewed, because failed programs are rarely published. Efficacy and toxicity depend on whole-body biology, differences between patients and long timescales that current models don't capture. Validating a prediction ultimately requires a trial, so feedback is slow and expensive.

As a result, AI-discovered drugs have shown high Phase I success rates, but their Phase II efficacy results so far look about the same as conventionally discovered drugs.

points.why: The response describes limited and unrepresentative training data without explaining that learning from existing patterns leaves unknown biological mechanisms beyond the model’s reach.
The response identifies toxicity as a cause of failure but does not attribute it to previously unknown effects of hitting a biological target.
The response describes choosing the wrong drug target and omitting known factors from models without establishing that researchers often cannot identify which variables or pathways to model.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Machine learning and computational methods have accelerated early drug discovery—such as predicting protein structures, finding hit compounds, and optimizing binding affinity—yet clinical trial failure rates remain stubbornly high, largely because the hardest bottleneck is human biology rather than molecular design. Most drugs fail in Phase II and III due to lack of efficacy or unforeseen toxicity, which typically reflects flawed target selection or an incomplete understanding of complex, multi-system disease pathways. Even a computationally perfected molecule will fail if modulating its target does not meaningfully alter the disease in diverse patient populations. Furthermore, machine learning models are only as good as their training data. Preclinical datasets from cell cultures and animal models are noisy, biased toward positive results, and notoriously poor predictors of human physiology, metabolism, and off-target effects. Finally, clinical validation is slow and expensive, producing tiny, often proprietary datasets that deny algorithms the rapid, high-volume feedback loops needed to learn what truly succeeds in humans.

points.why: The response identifies limitations in training data quality and quantity but does not explain that models cannot infer biological mechanisms absent from those data.
The response identifies unforeseen toxicity as a cause of clinical failure and links it to target selection or incomplete knowledge of biological pathways.
quotes: due to lack of efficacy or unforeseen toxicity
which typically reflects flawed target selection or an incomplete understanding of complex, multi-system disease pathways

points.why: The response discusses flawed target selection and incomplete biological understanding without stating that researchers struggle to identify which variables, pathways, or endpoints to model.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Machine learning can help researchers find promising molecules, but most clinical trials fail for reasons that are hard to predict from early discovery data. A compound can bind its intended target and work in cells or animals, yet fail to improve outcomes in patients. The target may play a different role in human disease than expected, the drug may never reach the relevant tissue at a tolerable dose, or side effects may emerge only after longer exposure or in a larger, more diverse population.

Models learn from the data available to them. Those data often contain few well-documented failures and provide limited evidence about how a new drug will affect different groups of patients. Trial design also matters: patient selection, dosing, and the choice of what to measure can determine whether a real benefit is detectable. Computational methods can improve which drugs enter trials, but showing that they substantially lower failure rates requires prospective evidence across many trials.

points.why: The response ties the limits of prediction to what the available data capture about failures and patient responses.
quotes: Models learn from the data available to them.
Those data often contain few well-documented failures and provide limited evidence about how a new drug will affect different groups of patients.

points.why: The response describes when side effects may emerge without attributing trial-ending toxicity to previously unknown target effects.
The response discusses what to measure in trials without saying that researchers often cannot identify which biological variables to model.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Machine learning can help researchers find compounds that bind to a target, but clinical success depends on a harder question: does changing that target improve patients’ health at a dose they can safely tolerate? A model can predict binding accurately even when the underlying theory of the disease is wrong.

Models learn largely from laboratory assays, animal studies, and historical trials. Those data capture only part of human biology, and failed studies are often unavailable for training. A drug that looks promising in the lab may never reach the affected tissue at an effective concentration, cause unexpected toxicity, or benefit only a subset of patients. Trials can also miss a real benefit if they enroll the wrong population or measure the wrong outcome. Computational methods can help teams choose better candidates and design better trials, but faster candidate selection alone does little to resolve the uncertainties that cause many drugs to fail in patients.

points.why: The response identifies gaps in training data but stops short of explaining that learning patterns from those data cannot reveal biological mechanisms the data do not capture.
The response identifies toxicity that emerges unexpectedly despite promising lab results as a reason drug candidates fail in patients.
quotes: A drug that looks promising in the lab

points.why: The response discusses incorrect disease theories and poorly chosen trial outcomes but does not say that researchers may be unable to identify the biological variables or pathways a model should include.
